questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical terminology)
questions.q: In the word tendinitis, what does the suffix -itis mean?
questions.explain: The suffix -itis means inflammation, so tendinitis is inflammation of a tendon. Surgical removal is -ectomy, softening is -malacia and enlargement is -megaly, which are common distractors because all four are frequent suffixes.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical terminology)
questions.q: A chart note documents bradypnea. What does the prefix brady- indicate?
questions.explain: Brady- means slow, so bradypnea is abnormally slow breathing. Tachy- means rapid, dys- means painful or difficult, and a- or an- means absent, as in apnea, which is the tempting confusion.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical terminology)
questions.q: Which term describes surgical removal of the gallbladder?
questions.explain: Cholecyst/o refers to the gallbladder and -ectomy means excision, so cholecystectomy is removal of the gallbladder. Cholecystotomy is an incision into it, cholelithiasis means gallstones and cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical abbreviations)
questions.q: A preprocedure order reads NPO after midnight. What does this instruct the patient to do?
options: Take all medicines by mouth after midnight
Take nothing by mouth after midnight
Eat only clear liquids after midnight
questions.explain: NPO comes from the Latin nil per os, meaning nothing by mouth. A clear liquid diet is a different order, and any exception for medicines must come from the provider, which is why the MA confirms questions with the provider.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical terminology)
questions.q: What does the term hypoglycemia mean?
questions.explain: Hypo- means below normal, glyc/o means sugar and -emia means a blood condition, so hypoglycemia is low blood glucose. High blood glucose is hyperglycemia, and glucose in the urine is glycosuria.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (directional terms)
questions.q: Which directional term means toward the midline of the body?
questions.explain: Medial means toward the midline, and lateral means away from it toward the side. Distal means farther from the point of attachment of a limb, and superficial means toward the body surface.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (health care settings)
questions.q: Which setting provides same-day surgery for patients who do not need an overnight hospital stay?
questions.explain: An ambulatory surgical center performs outpatient procedures and discharges patients the same day. Long-term care and skilled nursing facilities provide ongoing or rehabilitative care over days to years, and hospice focuses on comfort at the end of life.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (health care settings)
questions.q: What is the main focus of hospice care?
options: Curative treatment of the underlying disease
Comfort and quality of life near the end of life
Intensive rehabilitation after a major surgery
Stabilizing patients in an acute emergency
questions.explain: Hospice serves patients with a terminal illness and focuses on comfort, symptom control and support for the family rather than cure. Rehabilitation and emergency stabilization belong to other settings.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical specialties)
questions.q: A patient is referred for a changing mole on the back. Which specialist usually evaluates this concern?
questions.explain: Dermatology covers disorders of the skin, hair and nails, including suspicious moles. A nephrologist treats kidney disease, a podiatrist treats the feet and a hematologist treats blood disorders.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical specialties)
questions.q: Which physician specialty focuses on disorders of glands such as the thyroid and adrenal glands?
questions.explain: Endocrinology deals with hormone-producing glands, including the thyroid, adrenal glands and pancreas. Gastroenterology covers the digestive tract, rheumatology covers joints and autoimmune disease, and neurology covers the nervous system.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (pharmacology basics)
questions.q: Which drug classification is used to reduce fever?
questions.explain: An antipyretic lowers fever; acetaminophen is a common example. An antitussive suppresses cough, an anticoagulant reduces blood clotting and an antiemetic prevents nausea and vomiting.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (pharmacology basics)
questions.q: How does a drug's generic name differ from its brand name?
options: It is the trademarked name chosen and owned by the maker
It is the full chemical formula of the drug
It is the name of the drug class it belongs to
It is the nonproprietary name not owned by one company
questions.explain: The generic name is the official nonproprietary name that any manufacturer may use once the patent expires. The brand or trade name is owned by a company, and the chemical name describes the molecular structure.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical abbreviations)
questions.q: A medication sig includes the abbreviation b.i.d. How often is the medication taken?
questions.explain: B.i.d. stands for twice a day. T.i.d. means three times a day and q.i.d. means four times a day. Every other day should be written out in full because its old abbreviation is easily misread.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (pharmacology basics)
questions.q: Which route places a tablet under the tongue to dissolve?
questions.explain: Sublingual means under the tongue, where the drug is absorbed through the mucosa. Buccal places the tablet between the cheek and gum, transdermal uses a skin patch and intradermal is an injection into the dermis.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (pharmacology basics)
questions.q: A patient taking an antihistamine for allergies reports drowsiness. How is the drowsiness classified?
questions.explain: A side effect is an unintended effect that occurs along with the intended one, and drowsiness is a known side effect of many antihistamines. The therapeutic effect is relief of allergy symptoms, which is also the indication.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (nutrition)
questions.q: Which nutrient is the body's main source of quick energy?
questions.explain: Carbohydrates are broken down to glucose, the body's preferred quick fuel. Fat also supplies energy but is used more slowly; vitamins, minerals and water are essential but provide no calories.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (nutrition)
questions.q: Which vitamin does the skin produce when exposed to sunlight?
questions.explain: Ultraviolet light lets the skin make vitamin D, which helps the body absorb calcium. Vitamin C comes from fruits and vegetables, B12 mainly from animal foods and vitamin K partly from gut bacteria and leafy greens.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (nutrition)
questions.q: A patient on a low-sodium diet asks which food to limit. Which item is usually highest in sodium?
questions.explain: Processed foods such as canned soups are major sources of dietary sodium. Fresh fruit, plain cooked grains and fresh vegetables prepared without added salt are naturally low in sodium.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (nutrition)
questions.q: Which nutrient is needed mainly to build and repair body tissues?
questions.explain: Proteins supply amino acids used to build and repair muscle, skin and other tissues. Fiber aids digestion, sodium helps fluid balance and glucose is primarily an energy source.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (psychology of care)
questions.q: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which needs must generally be met first?
options: Physiological needs such as food and air
Esteem needs such as recognition and respect
questions.explain: Maslow placed physiological needs such as oxygen, food, water and rest at the base of the hierarchy. Safety follows, then love and belonging, esteem and finally self-actualization, which is reached only when lower needs are met.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (psychology of care)
questions.q: A newly diagnosed patient insists the lab must have mixed up the results and refuses to discuss treatment. Which defense mechanism is this?
questions.explain: Denial is refusing to accept a painful reality, which is common after a new diagnosis. Projection attributes one's own feelings to others, sublimation redirects impulses into acceptable activity and regression is a return to childlike behavior.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (psychology of care)
questions.q: A seriously ill patient says, "If I can just make it to my grandson's graduation, I will take better care of myself." Which stage of grief does this reflect?
questions.explain: In the Kubler-Ross model, bargaining involves trying to negotiate more time, often with promises. Anger shows as resentment, denial as refusal to believe, and acceptance as coming to terms with the situation.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical terminology)
questions.q: The combining form hepat/o refers to which organ?
questions.explain: Hepat/o means liver, as in hepatitis. The kidney is nephr/o or ren/o, the stomach is gastr/o and the spleen is splen/o.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Foundational Knowledge and Basic Science (medical terminology)
questions.q: What does the term hematuria describe?
questions.explain: Hemat/o means blood and -uria refers to urine, so hematuria is blood in the urine. Painful urination is dysuria, urination at night is nocturia and absence of urine is anuria.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (cardiovascular system)
questions.q: Which heart chamber pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for delivery to the body?
questions.explain: The left ventricle has the thickest wall and pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, and the atria receive blood returning to the heart.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (respiratory system)
questions.q: Where does gas exchange between inhaled air and the blood take place?
questions.explain: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the thin walls of the alveoli and surrounding capillaries. The trachea and bronchi only conduct air, and the pleura is the membrane surrounding the lungs.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (endocrine system)
questions.q: Which organ of the body produces insulin?
questions.explain: Beta cells in the pancreatic islets produce insulin, which lowers blood glucose. The liver stores glucose as glycogen, the adrenal glands make cortisol and epinephrine, and the thyroid makes thyroid hormones.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (blood)
questions.q: Which blood cells carry oxygen to the tissues?
questions.explain: Erythrocytes, or red blood cells, contain hemoglobin that binds oxygen. Leukocytes, including lymphocytes, fight infection, and thrombocytes, or platelets, help blood clot.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (urinary system)
questions.q: What is the microscopic functional unit of the kidney that filters blood and forms urine?
questions.explain: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons that filter blood and produce urine. A neuron is a nerve cell, the ureter carries urine to the bladder and an alveolus is an air sac in the lung.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (musculoskeletal system)
questions.q: Which structure attaches skeletal muscle to bone?
questions.explain: Tendons connect muscle to bone so that muscle contraction moves the skeleton. Ligaments connect bone to bone, cartilage cushions joints and a bursa is a fluid-filled sac that reduces friction.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (musculoskeletal system)
questions.q: Which condition involves loss of bone density that leaves bones fragile and prone to fracture?
questions.explain: Osteoporosis is a loss of bone mass and density, common in older adults, especially postmenopausal women. Osteoarthritis is joint cartilage wear, scoliosis is lateral spine curvature and gout is uric acid crystal buildup in joints.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (cardiovascular system)
questions.q: Long-term uncontrolled high blood pressure most directly raises the risk of which complication?
questions.explain: Chronic hypertension damages blood vessels and is a leading risk factor for stroke, heart attack, heart failure and kidney disease. It is not a direct cause of cataracts, bone loss or anemia.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (endocrine system)
questions.q: Which gland is called the master gland because it controls many other endocrine glands?
questions.explain: The pituitary gland at the base of the brain releases hormones that regulate the thyroid, adrenal glands and gonads. It is itself controlled by the hypothalamus.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (respiratory system)
questions.q: A patient describes wheezing and chest tightness that worsen with exercise and cold air. Which condition do these symptoms most suggest?
questions.explain: Asthma causes airway inflammation and narrowing that produce wheezing, chest tightness and shortness of breath, often triggered by exercise, cold air or allergens. Gout affects joints, hepatitis the liver and cystitis the bladder.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (digestive system)
questions.q: Where is bile stored until it is released into the small intestine?
questions.explain: The liver makes bile and the gallbladder stores and concentrates it, releasing it into the duodenum to help digest fats. The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and insulin, and the spleen filters blood.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (nervous system)
questions.q: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and smooth voluntary movement?
questions.explain: The cerebellum coordinates muscle movement, posture and balance. The medulla controls breathing and heart rate, the frontal lobe handles reasoning and voluntary motor planning, and the hypothalamus regulates temperature, hunger and hormones.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (endocrine system)
questions.q: What is the main cause of type 1 diabetes?
options: The pancreas makes little or no insulin
The body's cells resist normal insulin
The kidneys fail to filter glucose
questions.explain: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of the insulin-producing beta cells, so patients require insulin. Insulin resistance is the main feature of type 2 diabetes, which is the tempting confusion.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (cardiovascular system)
questions.q: Which type of blood vessel carries blood away from the heart?
questions.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, usually oxygenated except the pulmonary arteries. Veins and the smaller venules return blood to the heart, and lymphatic vessels carry lymph, not blood.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Anatomy and Physiology (integumentary system)
questions.q: Which layer of the skin is the outermost protective layer?
questions.explain: The epidermis is the outer layer and contains no blood vessels. The dermis beneath it holds vessels, nerves and glands, and the subcutaneous layer, also called the hypodermis, stores fat.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (temperature)
questions.q: Which temperature is commonly taught as the average normal oral temperature for an adult?
questions.explain: An average adult oral temperature of 98.6°F, or 37°C, is the traditional reference, with a normal range around it. A reading of 100.4°F or higher is commonly treated as a fever, so it is not normal.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (temperature)
questions.q: A patient had a tooth extracted this morning. Which temperature route should usually be avoided?
questions.explain: Recent oral surgery makes the oral route uncomfortable and may disturb the site, so another route is chosen. Temporal artery, tympanic and axillary routes do not involve the mouth.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (temperature)
questions.q: When taking a tympanic temperature on an adult, how is the outer ear pulled to straighten the canal?
questions.explain: For adults the pinna is pulled up and back to straighten the ear canal so the probe points at the tympanic membrane. For young children under about 3 years the ear is pulled down and back.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (pulse)
questions.q: Which pulse site is most often used for a routine adult pulse during intake?
questions.explain: The radial pulse on the thumb side of the wrist is easy to reach and comfortable for the patient. The carotid is used in emergencies, and femoral and popliteal pulses are mainly checked to assess circulation to the legs.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (pulse)
questions.q: During intake, an adult's radial pulse is irregular. How long should it be counted?
questions.explain: An irregular pulse can give a misleading result if counted for a short time and multiplied, so it is counted for a full minute. Many offices count regular pulses for 30 seconds and double the result.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (respirations)
questions.q: Why does the medical assistant keep the fingers on the wrist after counting the pulse while counting respirations?
options: So the pulse and respirations can be added together
So the patient's arm stays warm during the count
So the count can include the pulse pressure
So the patient does not change breathing on purpose
questions.explain: People often change their breathing pattern when they know it is being watched. Keeping the fingers in place lets the MA observe chest rise and fall discreetly for an accurate count.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (blood pressure)
questions.q: Which term describes the arterial pressure while the ventricles are contracting?
questions.explain: Systolic pressure is the peak pressure during ventricular contraction and is the top number. Diastolic pressure is measured while the ventricles relax, and pulse pressure is the difference between the two.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (blood pressure)
questions.q: What effect does using a blood pressure cuff that is too small for the patient's arm usually have?
questions.explain: A cuff bladder that is too narrow or short needs more pressure to compress the artery, producing a falsely high reading. A cuff that is too large tends to give a falsely low reading.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (blood pressure)
questions.q: How should a seated patient's arm be positioned for a blood pressure measurement?
questions.explain: The arm is supported with the cuff at heart level. An arm hanging below the heart gives a falsely high reading, and an arm held above heart level gives a falsely low reading.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (blood pressure)
questions.q: Before a routine seated blood pressure, how long is the patient commonly asked to rest quietly?
questions.explain: Common guidance is for the patient to sit quietly with feet flat and back supported for at least 5 minutes, without talking. Measuring right after walking in or talking can raise the reading.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (blood pressure)
questions.q: While listening during a manual blood pressure, which sound is recorded as the systolic pressure?
options: The point where all sound disappears
The point where sounds become muffled
The loudest sound heard during deflation
questions.explain: The first clear tapping sound, phase I of the Korotkoff sounds, marks systolic pressure. In adults the disappearance of sound, phase V, is usually recorded as the diastolic pressure.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (pulse oximetry)
questions.q: What does a pulse oximeter measure?
options: Carbon dioxide level in the blood
questions.explain: A pulse oximeter uses light passing through a finger or earlobe to estimate the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen, along with the pulse rate. It does not measure carbon dioxide or blood pressure.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (pulse oximetry)
questions.q: Which factor can interfere with a fingertip pulse oximeter reading?
options: Dark nail polish on the finger
questions.explain: Dark nail polish or artificial nails can block the light the sensor uses, as can cold fingers with poor circulation or movement. Sitting upright, drinking water and normal room temperature do not interfere.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (pulse oximetry)
questions.q: During intake, an adult who appears short of breath has a pulse oximeter reading of 86 percent on room air. What should the MA do?
options: Recheck the reading at the next visit
Document it and continue the intake
Have the patient walk the hallway
questions.explain: A saturation this low with shortness of breath is an abnormal finding that needs prompt attention. The MA reports it to the provider immediately rather than only documenting it or delaying care.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (height, weight and BMI)
questions.q: Which two measurements are used to calculate body mass index?
questions.explain: BMI is calculated from weight and height, as kilograms divided by meters squared or with an equivalent formula in pounds and inches. Waist circumference is a separate measure of abdominal fat.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (height, weight and BMI)
questions.q: An adult's BMI is 27. In the standard adult categories, how is this classified?
questions.explain: Standard adult categories classify a BMI of 25 to 29.9 as overweight, 18.5 to 24.9 as healthy weight and 30 or more as obese. A BMI of 27 therefore falls in the overweight range.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (height, weight and BMI)
questions.q: A patient weighs 66 kilograms. About how many pounds is this?
questions.explain: One kilogram equals about 2.2 pounds, so 66 multiplied by 2.2 is about 145 pounds. Dividing by 2.2 instead of multiplying gives 30, a common conversion error.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (height, weight and BMI)
questions.q: How is the length of an infant who cannot yet stand usually measured?
options: Lying flat on a measuring board
questions.explain: Infants are measured recumbent, from the crown of the head to the heel with the legs extended, often on a measuring board. Standing height is used once a child can stand straight without support.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (chief complaint)
questions.q: How is a patient's chief complaint best documented?
options: As a diagnosis in medical terms
As the MA's opinion of the cause
Briefly, in the patient's own words
As a full list of past illnesses
questions.explain: The chief complaint is the reason for the visit and is recorded concisely, often quoting the patient. The MA does not diagnose, and the past history is recorded in its own section.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (patient history)
questions.q: In which section of the health history is tobacco and alcohol use recorded?
questions.explain: Social history covers lifestyle factors such as tobacco, alcohol and drug use, occupation and living situation. Family history covers conditions of blood relatives, and the review of systems covers symptoms by body system.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (patient history)
questions.q: A patient's mother and brother both have type 2 diabetes. Where is this information recorded?
questions.explain: Health conditions of blood relatives are recorded in the family history because they can affect the patient's risk. The history of present illness describes the current problem in detail.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (pain assessment)
questions.q: A patient rates pain on a 0 to 10 scale. What should be documented?
options: The MA's own estimate of the pain level
Only whether the patient appears to be in pain
The number after rounding it down by one
The number the patient gives and the location
questions.explain: Pain is subjective, so the patient's own rating is recorded along with location and other details the patient describes. The MA does not substitute a personal estimate for the patient's report.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (orthostatic vital signs)
questions.q: In what order are positions commonly used when measuring orthostatic vital signs?
questions.explain: Orthostatic measurements usually start with the patient lying down, then sitting and then standing, with blood pressure and pulse taken in each position. A drop in pressure on standing can indicate orthostatic hypotension.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (pulse)
questions.q: Which pulse site is preferred for counting the heart rate of an infant?
questions.explain: The apical pulse, heard with a stethoscope over the apex of the heart, is the most accurate site in infants and is counted for a full minute. The radial pulse is hard to feel in infants.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Intake and Vitals (temperature)
questions.q: Which thermometer is gently swept across the forehead to take a reading?
questions.explain: A temporal artery thermometer scans the temporal artery across the forehead, often ending behind the ear per the manufacturer. A tympanic thermometer is placed in the ear canal.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (positioning)
questions.q: Which position is used for a pelvic examination?
questions.explain: In the lithotomy position the patient lies on the back with feet in stirrups and knees flexed, giving access to the pelvic area. Sims is a side-lying position, prone is face down and Fowler is a sitting position.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (positioning)
questions.q: A patient lies on the left side with the right knee drawn up toward the chest for a rectal examination. What is this position called?
questions.explain: The Sims position is left side-lying with the upper knee flexed and is used for rectal exams and some procedures. The knee-chest position has the patient kneeling with the chest on the table.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (positioning)
questions.q: A patient with shortness of breath is waiting for the provider. Which position usually makes breathing easier?
questions.explain: Raising the head of the table lets the diaphragm move more freely and eases breathing. Lying flat or with the head lowered pushes abdominal organs against the diaphragm and can worsen dyspnea.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (positioning)
questions.q: In which position does the patient lie face down?
questions.explain: Prone means lying face down and is used to examine the back or spine. Supine means lying on the back, dorsal recumbent is on the back with knees bent, and semi-Fowler is partly sitting.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (exam assisting)
questions.q: Which instrument does the provider use to look into the ear canal and at the eardrum?
questions.explain: An otoscope has a light and a speculum for viewing the ear canal and tympanic membrane. An ophthalmoscope views the interior of the eye, and a tuning fork tests hearing by vibration.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (exam assisting)
questions.q: Which instrument is used to test deep tendon reflexes?
questions.explain: A percussion or reflex hammer taps tendons such as the patellar tendon to check reflexes. The tuning fork tests hearing or vibration sense, and the tongue depressor helps view the throat.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (injections)
questions.q: At what angle is the needle inserted for an intramuscular injection?
questions.explain: Intramuscular injections are given at 90 degrees to reach muscle tissue. Subcutaneous injections are commonly given at 45 or 90 degrees depending on the needle and tissue, and intradermal injections at 10 to 15 degrees.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (injections)
questions.q: At what angle is the needle inserted for an intradermal injection such as a tuberculin skin test?
questions.explain: An intradermal injection is given at a shallow 10 to 15 degree angle with the bevel up, just under the epidermis. A 90 degree angle would place the medication in muscle instead.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (injections)
questions.q: Which site is generally preferred for intramuscular injections in infants?
questions.explain: The vastus lateralis on the anterolateral thigh is the preferred IM site for infants because it is well developed and away from major nerves. The deltoid is too small in infants and the dorsogluteal site risks sciatic nerve injury.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (injections)
questions.q: Which site is commonly used for small-volume intramuscular vaccines in adults?
questions.explain: The deltoid muscle of the upper arm is a common site for adult IM vaccines such as influenza vaccine. The abdomen is a subcutaneous site, the forearm is used for intradermal tests and the upper back is not an IM site.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (tuberculin skin test)
questions.q: When is a tuberculin skin test usually read?
questions.explain: The reaction to a tuberculin skin test develops over two to three days, so it is read 48 to 72 hours after placement. A test not read within that window usually has to be repeated.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (tuberculin skin test)
questions.q: How is the result of a tuberculin skin test measured?
questions.explain: The reader measures only the firm raised area, the induration, across the forearm in millimeters. Redness alone is not measured, which is a frequent error.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (injections)
questions.q: Which route is used for routine insulin injections?
questions.explain: Insulin for routine use is injected into the subcutaneous fat, usually of the abdomen, thigh or upper arm, for steady absorption. Intramuscular injection would absorb faster and less predictably.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (medication preparation)
questions.q: Before drawing medication from a multiple-dose vial, what is done to the rubber stopper?
questions.explain: The stopper is cleaned with alcohol and allowed to dry before the needle is inserted to reduce contamination. The stopper is never removed, which would break the vial's seal.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (medication preparation)
questions.q: Why is air equal to the dose injected into a vial before medication is withdrawn?
options: To prevent a vacuum that makes withdrawal hard
To sterilize the medication inside the vial
To dilute the medication to a safe strength
To mix two medications in the same vial
questions.explain: Adding air equal to the volume to be withdrawn keeps pressure balanced, so the liquid flows easily into the syringe. Air does not sterilize or dilute the medication.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (medication preparation)
questions.q: Which needle is used to draw medication from a glass ampule?
questions.explain: Breaking an ampule can leave tiny glass particles in the liquid, so a filter needle is used to draw it up and then replaced with a new needle for injection. Lancets and winged collection sets are for blood collection.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (injections)
questions.q: What is the purpose of the Z-track injection technique?
options: To keep medication from leaking into tissue
To give medication just under the epidermis
To speed absorption into the bloodstream
To reduce the amount of medication needed
questions.explain: Z-track displaces the skin before an IM injection so the needle track is sealed when the skin is released, keeping irritating or staining drugs in the muscle. It does not change dose or route.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (medication administration)
questions.q: Which item is one of the rights of medication administration?
questions.explain: The rights include right patient, drug, dose, route and time, with right documentation commonly added. The pharmacy, insurance and specialist are not among the rights checked before giving a drug.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (medication administration)
questions.q: As traditionally taught, how many times is a medication label checked against the order before it is given?
questions.explain: The label is checked when the medication is taken from storage, when it is prepared and before returning or giving it. Five refers to the classic number of rights, a common mix-up.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (medication administration)
questions.q: While preparing an injection, the MA notices the vial expired last month. What should be done?
options: Use it because potency lasts a full year
Do not use it and get an unexpired vial
Use it if the liquid still looks clear
Give half the dose from this vial only
questions.explain: Expired medications may be less effective or unsafe and must not be given, regardless of appearance. The MA obtains an unexpired supply and handles the expired vial according to office policy.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (vaccines)
questions.q: Under federal law, what must be given to a patient or parent before certain vaccines are administered?
options: A copy of the provider's state medical license
A consent form for the pharmacy
questions.explain: The National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act requires providers to give the current CDC Vaccine Information Statement before each dose of covered vaccines. The VIS explains benefits and risks in plain language.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (vaccines)
questions.q: At what temperature range are refrigerated vaccines stored according to CDC guidance?
questions.explain: CDC guidance keeps refrigerated vaccines between 2°C and 8°C, with temperatures monitored and logged. Freezing can destroy many refrigerated vaccines, which is why the freezer range is a tempting but wrong choice.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (injections)
questions.q: What is the correct handling of a needle right after an injection?
options: Recap it with both hands and discard it in the trash
Bend the needle and place it in a biohazard bag
Set it on the tray to discard after the visit
Activate the safety device and discard it in sharps
questions.explain: Used needles are not recapped by hand; the safety feature is activated and the needle goes immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container. Delaying disposal or bending needles increases needlestick risk.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (injections)
questions.q: Which sign shows that an intradermal injection was given correctly?
options: A small raised bleb at the site
A deep bruise under the skin
No visible change at the site
questions.explain: A correctly given intradermal injection forms a small pale raised bleb or wheal under the epidermis. No bleb suggests the medication went too deep.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (medication administration)
questions.q: A patient uses a medicated skin patch. What should be done with the old patch when a new one is applied?
options: Leave it on so the dose stays the same
Place the new patch over the old one
Remove it and apply the new one to another site
Remove it only after the new one starts working
questions.explain: The old patch is removed before applying a new patch to clean, dry skin at a different site. Leaving the old patch on can deliver extra medication, and rotating sites reduces skin irritation.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (medication administration)
questions.q: Where are ophthalmic drops instilled?
options: Directly onto the center of the cornea
Into the inner corner of the eyelid
questions.explain: The lower lid is gently pulled down and the drop placed into the conjunctival sac, avoiding touching the eye with the dropper. Dropping onto the cornea causes blinking and discomfort.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (wound care)
questions.q: Which type of wound drainage is thin, watery and clear?
questions.explain: Serous drainage is clear and watery. Sanguineous is bloody, serosanguineous is thin and pinkish, and purulent drainage is thick and often yellow or green, suggesting infection.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (wound care)
questions.q: A wound is draining thick yellow-green fluid with a foul odor. What does this most likely suggest?
questions.explain: Purulent drainage, especially with odor, redness or warmth, suggests infection and is reported to the provider. Normal healing drainage is usually serous or slightly pink.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (wound care)
questions.q: During a dressing change, what is done after the soiled dressing is removed?
options: Keep the same gloves on while applying the new clean dressing
Rinse the gloves under water and continue
Remove the gloves, do hand hygiene and put on new gloves
Add a second pair of gloves over the first
questions.explain: Gloves used to remove a soiled dressing are contaminated. They are removed, hand hygiene is performed and new gloves, sterile if required, are put on before the new dressing is applied.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (sterile technique)
questions.q: Which part of a sterile field is commonly considered unsterile?
questions.explain: The outer 1 inch of a sterile field is treated as contaminated because it may touch unsterile surfaces. Items are placed inside that border, and everything must stay above waist level and in sight.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (sterile technique)
questions.q: The MA turns away from a sterile field and cannot see it for a moment. How is the field considered?
options: Sterile, if no one touched it
Contaminated, because it was out of view
Sterile, if it stays covered later
Contaminated only if a spill occurred
questions.explain: A sterile field must remain in view at all times because contamination cannot be ruled out once it is out of sight. Turning away means the field is considered contaminated.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (sterile technique)
questions.q: When opening a sterile wrapped pack on a table, which flap is opened first?
questions.explain: The far flap is opened first so the MA does not reach over the exposed sterile contents. The side flaps follow, and the flap closest to the body is opened last.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (sterile technique)
questions.q: When pouring a sterile solution into a container on a sterile field, why is a small amount poured into a waste container first?
options: To cleanse the lip of the bottle
questions.explain: Pouring off a small amount, called lipping, rinses the bottle lip so contaminants are not carried into the sterile container. The solution is then poured without splashing, which would wick contamination.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (minor procedures)
questions.q: Where is a suture cut during removal?
options: At the farthest point from the knot
Halfway between the knot and skin
Below the knot, close to the skin
questions.explain: Cutting just under the knot near the skin lets the suture be pulled out without drawing the exposed outer portion through the tissue. This reduces infection risk.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (minor procedures)
questions.q: Which instrument is designed to clamp blood vessels during a minor procedure?
questions.explain: A hemostat has locking jaws for clamping vessels to control bleeding. A needle holder grasps suture needles, thumb forceps pick up tissue and a scalpel cuts tissue.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (eye irrigation)
questions.q: During eye irrigation, in which direction should the solution flow?
options: From the inner canthus toward the outer canthus
From the outer canthus toward the inner canthus
From the lower lid toward the upper lid
questions.explain: Solution flows from the inner corner near the nose toward the outer corner so debris and contaminants are carried away from the other eye and the tear duct.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (ear irrigation)
questions.q: During an adult ear irrigation, how is the solution directed?
options: Gently toward the upper wall of the canal
Toward the floor of the ear canal
Into the canal with the tip sealed tight
questions.explain: The stream is aimed gently at the roof of the canal so it flows behind the cerumen and out, while the pinna is pulled up and back. Aiming at the eardrum or sealing the canal can injure the eardrum.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (ear irrigation)
questions.q: Why is ear irrigation solution warmed to about body temperature?
options: To kill bacteria in the canal
To dissolve the wax right away
questions.explain: Solution that is much colder or warmer than body temperature can stimulate the inner ear and cause vertigo and nausea. Warming it does not sterilize the canal or anesthetize it.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (vision screening)
questions.q: For a distance visual acuity test with a standard Snellen chart, how far does the patient stand from the chart?
questions.explain: The standard Snellen chart is read from 20 feet, which is why results are written as 20 over a number. Near vision is tested separately with a handheld card at reading distance.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (vision screening)
questions.q: A patient's distance visual acuity is recorded as 20/40. What does this mean?
options: The patient sees at 40 feet what normal eyes see at 20
The patient sees at 20 feet what normal eyes see at 40
The patient read 20 of 40 letters correctly
The patient has 40 percent of normal vision
questions.explain: The top number is the testing distance and the bottom number is the distance at which a person with normal vision could read that line. A larger bottom number means poorer distance vision.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (vision screening)
questions.q: Which test screens for color vision deficiency?
questions.explain: Ishihara plates show numbers made of colored dots that people with certain color vision deficiencies cannot see. The Snellen chart tests distance acuity, the Jaeger card tests near vision and tonometry measures eye pressure.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (emergencies)
questions.q: A patient in the waiting room collapses and does not respond. After making sure the area is safe, what should the MA do next?
options: Give the patient water and wait a minute
Call for help and an AED, then check breathing
Move the patient to a chair before checking
Leave to find the provider's schedule
questions.explain: For an unresponsive person, the rescuer shouts for help, activates the emergency response, sends for an AED and checks breathing and pulse. If there is no normal breathing or pulse, CPR begins immediately.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (emergencies)
questions.q: A patient with diabetes is alert but shaky and sweaty, and a fingerstick shows low glucose. What is usually given per office protocol?
options: A fast-acting sugar such as juice
An injection of rapid-acting insulin now
questions.explain: An alert hypoglycemic patient who can swallow is commonly given about 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, such as juice or glucose tablets, per protocol, and glucose is rechecked. Insulin would lower the glucose further.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (emergencies)
questions.q: Minutes after an injection, a patient develops hives, wheezing and throat tightness. What should the MA do first?
options: Apply a cold pack and observe for an hour or so
Have the patient drive to urgent care
Alert the provider and start emergency response
Give an oral antihistamine and document it
questions.explain: Hives with breathing difficulty after an injection suggest anaphylaxis, a life-threatening emergency. The MA stays with the patient, summons the provider and emergency help, and follows the office anaphylaxis protocol.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (first aid)
questions.q: A patient has a deep cut on the forearm that is bleeding heavily. What is the first step to control bleeding?
options: Wash the wound well with hydrogen peroxide first
Apply firm direct pressure with a dressing
Apply ice directly to the open wound
Lower the arm below the heart
questions.explain: Firm direct pressure with a clean dressing is the first and most effective step to control external bleeding. A tourniquet is reserved for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure does not control.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (first aid)
questions.q: A patient spills hot coffee on the hand and has a small, minor burn. What first aid is appropriate?
options: Cool the area under cool running water
Apply ice directly to the burned skin
Spread butter over the burned skin
Break any blisters that have formed
questions.explain: Cooling a minor burn with cool running water helps stop the burning process and eases pain. Ice can damage tissue, butter traps heat and invites infection, and blisters should be left intact.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (emergencies)
questions.q: A patient has a generalized seizure on the exam room floor. What should the MA do?
options: Place a tongue blade between the teeth
Protect the head and time the seizure
Hold the arms and legs still
Give sips of water during the seizure
questions.explain: During a seizure, the MA moves objects away, cushions the head, does not restrain the patient or put anything in the mouth, and notes the time. The patient is turned on the side afterward and the provider is alerted.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (emergencies)
questions.q: When an AED is analyzing the heart rhythm, what should everyone do?
options: Keep giving chest compressions without pause
Stand clear and not touch the patient
Hold the pads firmly in place
questions.explain: Touching the patient during analysis can cause motion artifact and an incorrect analysis, and touching during a shock can injure the rescuer. Compressions resume right after the shock or the no-shock prompt.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (first aid)
questions.q: A patient's ankle was sprained an hour ago. What is a common effect of applying a cold pack?
options: More blood flow to the injured joint area
Faster bone healing in the area
questions.explain: Cold causes vasoconstriction, which reduces swelling, bleeding into tissue and pain in a fresh injury. Heat causes vasodilation and increased blood flow and is used later for stiffness.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (ambulatory aids)
questions.q: When fitting axillary crutches, about how much space is commonly left between the armpit and the crutch pad?
options: Six inches or more for comfort
questions.explain: A gap of about two to three finger widths keeps weight off the axilla and protects the nerves there. Patients are taught to bear weight on the hands, not the armpits.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: General Patient Care (pediatric medication)
questions.q: When giving liquid medication to an infant with a dropper or oral syringe, where is the liquid directed?
options: Along the inside of the cheek
Straight to the back of the throat
Onto the tip of the tongue
Into the front of the lips
questions.explain: Small amounts are given slowly toward the inner cheek, letting the infant swallow between amounts. Squirting toward the back of the throat can cause choking or aspiration.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (chain of infection)
questions.q: In the chain of infection, a patient with a weakened immune system represents which link?
questions.explain: The susceptible host is the person who can become infected, and immune weakness increases that risk. The reservoir is where the organism lives, and the portal of exit is how it leaves the reservoir.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (chain of infection)
questions.q: A contaminated doorknob passes bacteria from one person's hand to another. What is the doorknob called?
questions.explain: A fomite is an inanimate object that can carry infectious organisms, an example of indirect contact transmission. A vector is a living carrier such as a mosquito or tick.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (chain of infection)
questions.q: Vaccinating employees against hepatitis B breaks the chain of infection at which link?
questions.explain: Immunization makes the person resistant to the organism, so the susceptible host link is broken. PPE and hand hygiene mainly break the means of transmission.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (sanitization)
questions.q: What is sanitization in a medical office?
options: Destroying all microbes including bacterial spores
Killing most pathogens with a chemical soak
Storing sterile items in sealed pouches
Cleaning to remove debris and lower microbe counts
questions.explain: Sanitization, scrubbing instruments with detergent and water to remove blood and debris, is the first step before disinfection or sterilization. Destroying all microbes including spores is sterilization.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (sterilization)
questions.q: Which process destroys all microorganisms, including bacterial spores?
questions.explain: Sterilization eliminates all forms of microbial life, including spores. Disinfection kills most pathogens but not necessarily all spores, sanitization reduces microbial counts and antisepsis applies to living tissue.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (autoclave)
questions.q: What does an autoclave use to sterilize instruments?
questions.explain: An autoclave uses saturated steam under pressure to reach temperatures that kill all microorganisms, including spores. Detergent and water are used for sanitization before autoclaving.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (autoclave)
questions.q: After an autoclave cycle, the indicator tape on a pack has changed color. What does this show?
options: The pack is proven to be sterile
The instruments are free of debris
The pack was exposed to the cycle
questions.explain: Indicator tape shows only that the pack was exposed to the sterilizing conditions, not that sterility was achieved. Biological indicators with bacterial spores are used to verify that the cycle actually kills organisms.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (autoclave)
questions.q: Which method verifies that an autoclave cycle actually kills microorganisms?
options: The temperature gauge on the door
A visual check of the instruments
questions.explain: A biological indicator contains highly resistant bacterial spores; if they do not grow after the cycle, the autoclave is killing organisms. Tape and gauges show exposure to conditions but not killing.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (autoclave)
questions.q: Why are hinged instruments placed in the open position before autoclaving?
options: So they take up less space
So steam can reach all surfaces
questions.explain: Steam must contact every surface to sterilize it, so hinged instruments such as hemostats are left open or unlocked. Closed hinges can trap air and shield surfaces from the steam.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (sterile supplies)
questions.q: A sterile pack on the shelf has a small tear in its wrapper. What should be done?
options: Consider it contaminated and reprocess it
Use it if the tear is under one inch long
Tape the tear closed and use it
Use it only for nonsterile procedures
questions.explain: Any break in the wrapper, moisture or other damage means sterility cannot be assured. The pack is considered contaminated and is rewrapped and sterilized again before use.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (hand hygiene)
questions.q: When using an alcohol-based hand rub, when is the process complete?
options: As soon as the product has been applied to the palms
After the hands are rinsed with water
After the hands are wiped with a towel
When hands are dry after rubbing all surfaces
questions.explain: The rub is applied to all surfaces of the hands and fingers and rubbed until dry. Rinsing or toweling it off reduces its effectiveness.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (hand hygiene)
questions.q: During handwashing, for how long does CDC guidance recommend rubbing the hands with soap?
questions.explain: CDC guidance calls for scrubbing all surfaces of the hands with soap for at least 20 seconds before rinsing. Shorter times leave more organisms; much longer times are associated with surgical scrubs.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (hand hygiene)
questions.q: Why is hand hygiene still needed after gloves are removed?
options: Hands may be soiled during removal or by glove defects
Gloves make the skin too dry for patient care
Gloves leave a powder residue that irritates the skin of patients
Hand hygiene is only needed if gloves tore visibly
questions.explain: Gloves can have tiny defects, and hands can become contaminated while taking gloves off. Hand hygiene after glove removal is part of standard precautions even when gloves appear intact.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (standard precautions)
questions.q: Under standard precautions, how is every patient's blood and body fluid treated?
options: As safe unless a diagnosis is known
As infectious only if visibly bloody
As safe if the patient feels well
questions.explain: Standard precautions treat blood, body fluids except sweat, nonintact skin and mucous membranes of all patients as potentially infectious, because infections are often unknown. Precautions do not depend on a diagnosis.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (PPE)
questions.q: The provider will irrigate a wound and splashing is likely. Which PPE should the assisting MA wear?
options: Gloves only, because the skin is protected
Gloves, gown, and face and eye protection
A face mask only, because hands are washed
A gown only, because gloves slow the work
questions.explain: When splashes or sprays of body fluids are expected, standard precautions call for gloves plus a gown and protection for the eyes, nose and mouth such as a mask with goggles or a face shield.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (transmission-based precautions)
questions.q: A patient with suspected measles arrives at the clinic. Which precaution category applies?
questions.explain: Measles spreads through tiny airborne particles that stay suspended, so airborne precautions are used along with standard precautions, ideally with an airborne infection isolation room and fit-tested respirators.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (transmission-based precautions)
questions.q: Which transmission-based precaution category is used for pertussis?
questions.explain: Pertussis spreads by large respiratory droplets during close contact, so droplet precautions with a mask are used along with standard precautions. Airborne precautions are for diseases such as measles and tuberculosis.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (OSHA)
questions.q: Under OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard, who pays for required personal protective equipment?
questions.explain: OSHA requires employers to provide appropriate PPE at no cost to employees with occupational exposure, and to make sure it is available in the right sizes. Employees must use it as trained.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (OSHA)
questions.q: Under OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard, which label is required on containers of regulated waste?
options: A green label reading general waste in black letters
A blue label with a recycling symbol
The biohazard symbol in orange or orange-red
A plain white label with the date
questions.explain: OSHA requires warning labels that are fluorescent orange or orange-red with the biohazard symbol, or red bags or containers may be used instead. Ordinary trash labels do not meet the requirement.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (OSHA)
questions.q: Where may employees eat and drink in a medical office under OSHA rules?
options: At the lab counter if gloves are off
Only in areas away from exposure risk
Anywhere if hands were just washed
questions.explain: OSHA prohibits eating, drinking, applying cosmetics and handling contact lenses in work areas where exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials is likely. Break areas are kept separate.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (disinfection)
questions.q: Why must a surface disinfectant stay wet for the contact time listed on the label?
options: To keep the surface from staining or fading
To make the surface less slippery
To let the odor fade before use
To kill the organisms the label claims
questions.explain: The label contact time is how long the product must remain wet to kill the listed organisms. Wiping a surface dry too soon may leave it inadequately disinfected.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (respiratory hygiene)
questions.q: A patient who is coughing and sneezing arrives at the front desk. Which respiratory hygiene step is appropriate?
options: Offer a mask and seat the patient apart
Ask the patient to wait outside the building
Reschedule the visit for next month
Give the patient hand lotion to use
questions.explain: Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette include offering a mask, tissues and hand hygiene supplies and separating coughing patients from others when possible.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (asepsis)
questions.q: What is the goal of medical asepsis?
options: Keeping a sterile field during surgery
Reducing the number and spread of microbes
questions.explain: Medical asepsis, or clean technique, reduces microorganisms and prevents their spread through hand hygiene, cleaning and PPE. Surgical asepsis aims to keep an area free of all microorganisms.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (regulated waste)
questions.q: Which item belongs in a red biohazard bag rather than regular trash?
options: A used tongue depressor with no blood
questions.explain: Items saturated or caked with blood that could release it if compressed are regulated waste. Items without blood or other potentially infectious material can usually go in regular trash per facility policy.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Infection Control (health care-associated infection)
questions.q: What is an infection acquired while receiving care in a health care setting called?
questions.explain: A health care-associated infection, sometimes called nosocomial, is acquired during care in a health care facility. Community-acquired infections are acquired outside health care settings.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (CLIA)
questions.q: What does it mean when a test is classified as CLIA-waived?
options: It does not need to follow any instructions at all
It can only be done in a hospital lab
It is simple and has low risk of a wrong result
It is exempt from all quality control
questions.explain: Waived tests are simple tests with a low risk of an erroneous result. Sites need a CLIA certificate of waiver and must follow the manufacturer's instructions, including any quality control steps.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (urinalysis)
questions.q: Which urine specimen is usually preferred for a urine pregnancy test because it is most concentrated?
questions.explain: Urine collected first in the morning has been concentrating overnight and contains the highest level of hCG, making early pregnancy easier to detect. A random specimen may be too dilute.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (urinalysis)
questions.q: Why are urine reagent strip results read at the exact times stated by the manufacturer?
options: The strip loses its color after one minute
The patient needs the result right away
Colors keep changing and late reads are wrong
The urine cools and stops reacting
questions.explain: Each pad develops color at its own rate, and reading too early or too late can give false results. Results are compared with the color chart at the times listed on the container.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (urinalysis)
questions.q: A routine urine specimen cannot be tested within about an hour of collection. What is commonly done?
questions.explain: Urine left at room temperature changes as bacteria multiply, cells break down and pH rises. Refrigeration slows these changes until the specimen can be tested, which is commonly taught as within an hour otherwise.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (glucose testing)
questions.q: Before a fingerstick glucose test, why should the patient's finger be clean and dry?
options: Wet skin makes the lancet go too deep
Dry skin keeps the meter from overheating
Clean skin makes the strip last longer
Residue or moisture can change the result
questions.explain: Sugar from food or fruit on the skin can falsely raise the result, and leftover alcohol or water can dilute the sample. The finger is washed or cleansed and allowed to dry fully.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (hematology)
questions.q: What does a microhematocrit measure?
options: The number of white cells in a microliter of blood
The time it takes the blood to clot
The amount of glucose in the plasma
The percentage of blood made up of red cells
questions.explain: Spinning blood in a capillary tube separates red cells from plasma, and the packed red cell volume is read as a percentage of the total. It does not count white cells or measure clotting.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (rapid strep)
questions.q: Where is the swab collected for a rapid strep antigen test?
options: The inside of the front of the nose
The back of the throat and the tonsils
The inner surface of the cheek
questions.explain: The swab is rubbed over the posterior pharynx and tonsils, avoiding the tongue, cheeks and teeth, which could dilute the specimen with saliva. A tongue depressor helps keep the swab clear.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (rapid strep)
questions.q: A child's rapid strep antigen test is negative. What is commonly done next per guidelines and office protocol?
options: Tell the family the child has strep
Send a throat culture to confirm
Repeat the rapid test on the same swab
questions.explain: Rapid antigen tests can miss some infections, so for children and adolescents a negative result is commonly followed by a throat culture, according to provider orders and protocol.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (quality control)
questions.q: When should quality control be run on a waived test system?
options: As the maker directs, such as with new lots
Only when a patient complains of a result
Only once when the system is first bought
Never, because waived tests need no controls
questions.explain: Waived testing sites must follow manufacturer instructions, which commonly call for controls with each new lot or shipment and at set intervals, plus any facility policy requirements.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (quality control)
questions.q: A control result for a glucose meter falls outside its acceptable range. What should be done?
options: Test patients and note the control result
Adjust patient results by the difference
Throw out the meter and order a new one
questions.explain: An out-of-range control means patient results may be inaccurate, so patient testing stops until the cause is found, corrective action is taken and controls fall within range. The action is documented.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (fecal occult blood)
questions.q: Which test detects hidden blood in a stool specimen?
questions.explain: A fecal occult blood or fecal immunochemical test detects blood not visible to the eye and is used to screen for colorectal cancer and other bleeding. The other tests do not examine stool.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (urinalysis)
questions.q: What does urine specific gravity indicate?
questions.explain: Specific gravity compares the density of urine with water and reflects how concentrated it is, which relates to hydration and kidney function. Acidity is measured by pH.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (urinalysis)
questions.q: Ketones appear on the urine strip of a patient with diabetes. What does this suggest?
options: The patient drank too much water
The body is burning fat for energy
questions.explain: Ketones form when the body breaks down fat because it cannot use glucose, which can occur with poorly controlled diabetes or fasting. The finding is reported to the provider.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (specimen handling)
questions.q: Where should the label be placed on a urine specimen container?
options: On the side of the container
On the bag holding the cup
questions.explain: Labels go on the container itself, not the lid, because lids are removed during testing and can be mixed up. The label matches the requisition with the patient identifiers, date and time.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Clinical Patient Care: Point-of-Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures (pregnancy testing)
questions.q: Which hormone does a urine pregnancy test detect?
questions.explain: Urine pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone produced by the developing placenta after implantation. Luteinizing hormone is detected by ovulation tests.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (referrals)
questions.q: The provider orders a referral to a cardiologist. What should the MA typically do?
options: Tell the patient to find a cardiologist alone
Schedule the visit without any paperwork
Check plan rules and send the needed records
Wait for the patient to request the referral
questions.explain: Processing a referral usually includes checking whether the insurance plan requires a referral or authorization, sending the order and relevant records to the specialist, and helping arrange the appointment.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (referrals)
questions.q: Why does an office track referrals after they are sent?
options: To bill the specialist a fee for each referral that is sent
To limit how many specialists a patient sees
To confirm the patient was seen and results returned
To remove the patient from the schedule
questions.explain: Tracking closes the loop: staff confirm that the appointment happened and that the consult report reached the ordering provider. Untracked referrals can lead to missed diagnoses and delayed care.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (preventive care)
questions.q: Which is an example of primary prevention?
options: Cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack
questions.explain: Primary prevention stops disease before it starts, as immunizations do. Screening such as mammography is secondary prevention, and rehabilitation after a disease event is tertiary prevention.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (preventive care)
questions.q: A colonoscopy is done to find early colon cancer in a patient who has no symptoms. What level of prevention is this?
questions.explain: Screening tests that detect disease early in people without symptoms are secondary prevention. Primary prevention prevents disease from occurring, and tertiary prevention limits complications of existing disease.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (barriers to learning)
questions.q: A patient who speaks limited English needs instructions for a new medication. What is the best approach?
options: Ask the patient's child to interpret
Speak more loudly and slowly in English
Give English handouts to read at home
questions.explain: A qualified medical interpreter conveys information accurately and confidentially. Family members, especially children, may omit or change information, and speaking louder does not overcome a language barrier.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (patient education)
questions.q: What is the teach-back method?
options: The MA reads the instructions aloud twice
The patient signs a form showing the handout was received
The patient explains the instructions in their own words
The provider repeats the plan at the next visit
questions.explain: Teach-back asks the patient to restate or demonstrate what they learned, which confirms understanding and reveals gaps to correct. Signing a form does not show understanding.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (patient education)
questions.q: A patient learns best by doing. How should the MA teach the use of a metered-dose inhaler?
options: Give a written handout for the patient to read at home
Describe the steps once over the phone
Demonstrate it, then have the patient practice
Show a picture of an inhaler in use
questions.explain: A kinesthetic learner benefits from a demonstration followed by a return demonstration, which lets the MA correct technique on the spot. Handouts and descriptions alone suit other learning styles.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (health literacy)
questions.q: Which approach best helps a patient with limited health literacy understand instructions?
options: Plain language and a few key points
A long handout with every detail
Fast speech to save the patient time
questions.explain: Plain language, focusing on two or three key actions, and checking understanding are recommended for limited health literacy. Jargon and long, dense materials make instructions harder to follow.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (barriers to learning)
questions.q: An older patient with poor eyesight needs written home care instructions. What helps most?
options: Instructions sent only by text message
questions.explain: Large, clear fonts with strong contrast and short sections are easier to read for patients with visual impairment. Reviewing the instructions aloud also helps.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (community resources)
questions.q: A patient mentions that she often cannot afford enough food. What can the MA do within the office's role?
options: Tell her the office cannot help with this kind of topic
Share information on local food assistance programs
Change her diet order to cost less money
Give her money from the office petty cash
questions.explain: Connecting patients with community resources, such as food assistance programs, is part of care coordination. The MA follows office protocol and informs the provider, who may address related health concerns.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (care plans)
questions.q: What is the MA's role in a patient's treatment plan?
options: Create the plan and choose medications
Change the plan if the patient asks
Explain the diagnosis before the provider
Reinforce the provider's plan within scope
questions.explain: The provider develops the treatment plan. The MA supports it by reinforcing instructions, scheduling follow-up and referring questions back to the provider, staying within scope of practice.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (care coordination)
questions.q: Why might an MA review the next day's schedule for care gaps before patients arrive?
options: To decide which patients are allowed to skip their visit
To change appointment times without notice
To find overdue screenings to address at the visit
To cancel visits for patients with balances
questions.explain: Previsit planning identifies overdue screenings, immunizations or tests so they can be addressed during the visit. It improves preventive care and makes visits more efficient.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (transitions of care)
questions.q: After a patient is discharged from the hospital, why might the office call the patient?
options: To tell the patient to stop all medications
To collect payment for the hospital stay
To ask the patient to rate the hospital
To help schedule follow-up and route questions
questions.explain: Follow-up calls after discharge help make sure the patient has a follow-up appointment and understands instructions, with medication or symptom questions routed to the provider. This reduces readmissions.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (care models)
questions.q: What best describes a patient-centered medical home?
options: A home health agency that visits patients at home
A nursing home that offers medical care
A hospital unit for long-term patients
A primary care team that coordinates all care
questions.explain: A patient-centered medical home is a primary care model in which a team led by the provider coordinates comprehensive, continuous care, including referrals and follow-up. It is not a physical residence.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (patient education)
questions.q: A patient who smokes says he is not ready to quit. What approach is most appropriate?
options: Respect his view and offer help for later
Insist that he quit before leaving today
Avoid the topic at all future visits
Tell him the provider will stop seeing him
questions.explain: Meeting patients where they are, offering information and leaving the door open supports future change. Pressure or threats can damage trust, and ignoring the topic misses later opportunities.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (patient education)
questions.q: After teaching a patient about home glucose testing, what should the MA document?
options: Only that a printed handout was given to the patient
What was taught and how the patient understood
Only the time of the teaching
Nothing, as teaching is not charted
questions.explain: Documentation includes the topic taught, materials provided and the patient's understanding, such as a successful return demonstration. Patient education is part of the legal record of care.

questions.ref: NHA CCMA test plan, Patient Care Coordination and Education (patient education)
questions.q: A patient is anxious after hearing a new diagnosis and has trouble remembering details. What helps most?
